paper.title_en: Light-particle emission in nucleon-induced fission of $^{235,238}$U at energies from 10 MeV to 1 GeV
paper.abstract_en: Background: In nucleon-induced fission up to GeV energies, early nonequilibrium emission alters the residual nuclei before statistical evaporation and scission. The emitted light particles therefore probe each reaction stage while supplying needed nuclear data. Purpose: We study neutron and light charged-particle emission in $^{235,238}$U$(n,f)$ and $^{235,238}$U$(p,f)$ reactions at incident energies from 10 MeV to 1 GeV. Methods: The reactions are simulated event by event by coupling the isospin-dependent quantum molecular dynamics model with the GEMINI++ statistical decay code. Results: The calculations follow the measured rise in average neutron multiplicity with incident energy, while yielding higher values above 100 MeV and in the proton-induced prescission component. Within the coupled calculations, the neutron multiplicity growth comes mainly from statistical evaporation before scission, whereas emission from the fission fragments changes weakly. Although the average preequilibrium neutron yield remains small, early emission spreads the residual nuclei across multiple elements and wide excitation energies. At high energies, protons are emitted predominantly before equilibration, directly reducing the charge retained by the residual nuclei. Conclusions: In the coupled calculations, statistical evaporation before scission governs the neutron multiplicity growth, whereas early nonequilibrium emission shapes the residual nuclei and dominates high-energy proton emission. These results provide a reference for modeling intermediate-energy fission, in which prescission emission changes the charge, mass, and excitation energy of the fissioning system.
